title: Wait for the reversal, not for a guessed time

blocks.text: An integration test checks that a reversal leaves the store-and-forward queue and reaches the host. The SAF sends on its own thread, so the test asks the host's log for it: `awaitReceived("0420", 5000)`. The test host puts every message it receives, in order, on a Space queue, and `HostLog` in `src/main/java/com/example/practice/HostLog.java` reads that queue.

The test fails about once in twenty runs on the build server and never on a laptop. Nobody has found the cause, so the team re-runs the build until it passes. `awaitReceived` sleeps half a second and then looks once.

Rewrite `awaitReceived`, the one method marked `TODO`. It returns the next message of the asked type, as soon as the host has it, and gives up when the time the test allowed is over. Network messages such as echoes can reach the host at any moment and are not what the test is waiting for. When the message doesn't come, the failure must say so in the test that waited, not as a `NullPointerException` three lines later. About ten lines.
Some of the tests deliver a message only after your code has started looking for it.

cases.says: a message of the asked type that the host has already received is returned
a message that arrives only after the wait has begun is still returned, because the wait lasts until it comes or the time is up
a message of another type that arrives first, such as an echo, is not taken for the one the test waits for
when the message never comes the wait fails with a TimeoutException instead of returning null

origin.section: 10.4 A Test Waits for a Condition, Never for a Time

concepts: q2.ready means deployed, not connected; a test waits for the condition it needs with a blocking read bounded by a deadline, never for a guessed time, and fails loudly when the deadline passes.
